q: A process of making a magnetic material into a magnet is called ____.
e: Magnetisation is the process by which a previously unmagnetised magnetic material is converted into a magnet.

q: Two types of magnetisation are (i) magnetisation by stroking and (ii) magnetisation using ____ current.
e: Magnetisation can be achieved either by physical stroking with a permanent magnet or by using a direct electric current.

q: Two types of magnetisation are (i) magnetisation by ____ and (ii) magnetisation using direct current.
e: Magnetisation can be achieved either by physical stroking with a permanent magnet or by using a direct electric current.

q: The best way to make powerful magnets is to use the magnetic effect of an ____ current.
e: Electromagnetism provides the most effective method for creating powerful magnets by passing an electric current through a coil.

q: A steel bar is placed inside a solenoid and a direct current is passed through the ____.
e: A solenoid is a coil of wire that generates a strong, uniform magnetic field when a direct current passes through it.

q: A steel bar is placed inside a solenoid and a ____ current is passed through the solenoid.
e: Direct current is required to create a steady magnetic field in the solenoid for permanent magnetisation.

q: The solenoid produces a magnetic field that magnetises the steel bar permanently (____ magnet).
e: Steel retains the magnetism induced by the solenoid's magnetic field even after the current is removed, becoming a permanent magnet.

q: The solenoid produces a ____ field that magnetises the steel bar permanently (permanent magnet).
e: The solenoid produces a magnetic field that magnetises the steel bar permanently (permanent magnet).

q: When the current through the solenoid is switched off, the steel bar stays ____.
e: Steel is a hard magnetic material, so it retains its magnetisation even after the external magnetic field is removed.

q: When the current through the solenoid is switched ____, the steel bar stays magnetised.
e: When the current through the solenoid is switched off, the steel bar stays magnetised.

q: If an iron bar is placed instead of steel bar, the iron bar becomes magnetised temporarily (____).
e: Iron is a soft magnetic material, so it only acts as a magnet while the current is flowing, functioning as an electromagnet.

q: If an iron bar is placed instead of steel bar, the iron bar becomes magnetised ____ (electromagnet).
e: Iron loses its magnetism quickly once the external magnetic field is removed, making it suitable for temporary magnetisation.

q: The polarities of the magnet produced depend on the direction of electric ____.
e: The north and south poles of an electromagnet are determined by the direction in which the electric current flows through the coil.

q: The polarities of the magnet produced depend on the ____ of electric current.
e: Reversing the direction of the electric current will reverse the polarities of the resulting magnet.

q: The bar is stroked several times in the same direction along its ____.
e: Stroking along the length of the bar aligns the internal magnetic domains in a uniform direction.

q: The magnet (or) magnets must be lifted high above the bar between successive ____.
e: Lifting the magnet high above the bar prevents the reverse stroke from demagnetising or misaligning the domains.

q: The end of the steel bar where the strokes finish always has the opposite polarity to that of the end of the stroking magnet in ____ with it.
e: The finishing end of the bar acquires a polarity opposite to the pole of the stroking magnet that was last in contact with it.

q: The end of the steel bar where the strokes finish always has the opposite ____ to that of the end of the stroking magnet in contact with it.
e: The finishing end of the bar acquires a polarity opposite to the pole of the stroking magnet that was last in contact with it.

q: When a piece of unmagnetised magnetic material (such as iron or steel) is brought near to the pole of a permanent magnet, it is attracted to the magnet and becomes a magnet ____.
e: The presence of a permanent magnet induces temporary magnetism in the nearby magnetic material, turning it into a magnet itself.

q: When a piece of unmagnetised magnetic material (such as iron or steel) is brought near to the pole of a permanent magnet, it is ____ to the magnet and becomes a magnet itself.
e: The unmagnetised material is attracted to the permanent magnet due to the induced opposite pole at the near end.

q: This is called induced ____.
e: The phenomenon where a magnetic material becomes magnetised due to the proximity of another magnet is called induced magnetism.

q: The material is said to have magnetism ____ in it.
e: The material is said to have magnetism induced in it by the external magnetic field.

q: In Figure 10.10 the north pole of the permanent magnet induces an S-pole in the near end of the soft iron while the far end of the soft iron becomes an ____.
e: Magnetic induction creates an opposite pole at the near end and a like pole at the far end of the induced magnet.

q: In Figure 10.10 the north pole of the permanent magnet induces an ____ in the near end of the soft iron while the far end of the soft iron becomes an N-pole.
e: Magnetic induction creates an opposite pole (S-pole) at the near end when a north pole is brought close.
